The Fender Stratocaster is widely considered to be the best-known shape in electric guitars

Hans Thomann leads the way through his music store in central Germany to the large electric guitar department, where the walls are hung with hundreds of instruments.

Brands on show include famous names Fender and Gibson, plus Harley Benton.

The latter is a low-price range of guitars owned by the family-run company that Thomann leads – Thomann, one of the world's largest online retailers of musical instruments.

The shop, together with warehouses and offices, are at the company's headquarters in the tiny village of Treppendorf in rural Upper Franconia, in Bavaria.

The business was founded by Thomann's father, Hans Thomann Senior, in 1954.

In one corner of the store, a young man is trying out a Fender Stratocaster, one of the world's most iconic electric guitars.

Designed in the US in the early 1950's, the "Strat" became the instrument of choice for many famous rock and pop musicians, such as Jimi Hendrix, Eric Clapton and Buddy Holly.

Hendrix famously set one on fire at the Monterey Pop Festival in 1967, and his performances helped make the guitar a symbol of modern rock music.

Hans Thomann says that Fender's letter came as a big surprise

These days, the Stratocaster is very much on Hans Thomann's mind, because it's the subject of an intense copyright dispute.

When the guitar was first made, California-based Fender did not trademark the body shape. So, since the 1960s Strat-shaped guitars have been made and sold around the world by countless manufacturers.

The shape is so ubiquitous that many musicians consider it to be a generic design.

But since March of this year, Fender has begun a new campaign to defend its right to the guitar's sinuous shape. It follows a decision by a court in Düsseldorf last December which granted Fender copyright protection , external of the Stratocaster design in Germany.

The defendant, Chinese seller Yiwu Philharmonic Musical Instruments, did not appear. The Düsseldorf court accepted Fender's arguments and ruled in its favour. According to German law the court makes its decision based on the facts presented by the plaintiff if the defendant doesn't raise objections.

The ruling said that Fender's design for the Stratocaster was "an outstanding, free creative achievement" that "clearly reflects the personality of its author".

It described the guitar as "a body without edges" with "soft curves that evoke associations with the female torso consisting of hips, waist and arms".

On its website, Fender announced in March , external the decision created "enforceable rights" against any guitars using the Strat body shape, that are manufactured, sold or distributed into Germany or other EU countries, "regardless of where those guitars are produced".

Fender began to send out cease and desist letters to dozens of retailers and manufacturers, both large and small, asking them to stop making and selling Strat lookalikes heading for Europe.

One of these letters, seen by the BBC, said Fender "insists that you immediately stop manufacturing, marketing, selling and producing the infringing products".

The letter also demanded that companies recall and destroy the guitars.

Jimi Hendrix helped to make the Fender Stratocaster famous

The move caused an outcry in the guitar world, among manufacturers and musicians.

"Time to boycott Fender," one person wrote on the Facebook page of the boutique US guitar maker, LSL Instruments.

Thomann received a cease-and-desist letter shortly after a visit to Treppendorf in March by Fender's chief executive Bud Cole.

"We remember the meeting as a very positive and constructive exchange," says Thomann. "At the time we had no indication that Fender was considering legal action."

"For more than 70 years, we have carried Fender instruments with great appreciation for the brand and many of us are Fender players ourselves. We were therefore surprised and disappointed by Fender's recent actions."

In 2025, Thomann sold over 112,000 Strat-style guitars, including more than 16,000 made by Fender and Fender subsidiary brand Squier.

"As a retailer, we want to continue offering our customers everything that is available in the world of guitars," adds Thomann. "We would have welcomed to the opportunity to discuss the matter openly before receiving a formal legal demand for such extreme action."

Thomann has just one physical shop, but sells online around the world

In June, Thomann the company started legal action against Fender, filing an "action of non-infringement" that said that Fender does not have a valid copyright claim to the Stat shape.

Thomann says that the Düsseldorf ruling was simply a default judgement based on missed deadlines and didn't represent a "comprehensive review of the legal claims".

For its part, Fender, which is majority-owned by Hawaii-based company Servco Pacific, says it has a responsibility to protect the Stratocaster's iconic design. In July, it sued Thomann in a German court, for copyright infringement.

In a statement to the BBC, Fender said it remained "confident" in the original Düsseldorf court judgement.

"Our preference has always been to keep lines of communication open and resolve these matters through constructive dialogue rather than litigation," it added.

With the legal cases continuing, Thomann says he believes it is important to get "legal clarity – not only for us but for the wider guitar industry."

"Ultimately, we want to help preserve an environment in which innovation, diversity and creative development can continue to thrive," he adds.

The Stratocaster is the most used emoji for a guitar

Thomann says he was taking legal action not just for his company, but for smaller music companies too.

"We used to be a small music shop ourselves," he says.

"Many of the smaller manufacturers, guitar makers and dealers affected simply don't have the financial and legal resources to conduct a legal dispute like this."

One such company is LSL Instruments, a family-owned boutique guitar maker in California. Its director of sales, Johny Miller, told me that when they first received Fender's letter they were "pretty terrified and blown away".

"They were asking us to retrieve guitars from dealers out there and destroy them and send them proof.

"So when we heard Hans Thomann got the same letter and responded by suing them… so that everybody in the guitar community could understand exactly what's going on… we were so thankful and grateful," he says.

Fender tells BBC that it agrees that "legal clarity was important", and that it was now focusing more on targeting larger manufacturers.

It also says it realises that "our outreach has caused concern and frustration, particularly among smaller, independent guitar builders. "To them we say: we continue to hear you, and we're listening."

Three pens and a red as Man Utd draw against Sporting

Two games, no wins. Two red cards, two goals scored. One goal disallowed, six conceded. Is it possible for Mauricio Pochettino to have learned anything from a crazy first week as Manchester United boss?

United and Pochettino went on the warpath before the Champions League encounter with Sporting, furious at Leny Yoro's dismissal at Liverpool which they believe was unjust and shaped the eventual 4-0 defeat.

Club officials were seething after the 2-2 draw in Lisbon as well.

This time it was 2022 World Cup final referee Szymon Marciniak in the firing line. Blowing before Amad's first-half header went into the net meant VAR had no chance to assess whether the Polish official was right to rule Youri Tielemans had fouled Goncalo Inacio before prodding the ball through to the Ivorian.

Former United winger Ashley Young didn't think so. He called Marciniak's performance "a disgrace".

That Tielemans picked up a booking that eventually led to his late red card – the Old Trafford outfit have now had four players sent off in their past five games, meaning the Belgian will miss the Old Trafford clash with RB Leipzig on 8 December - just compounded the situation.

Then, in a matter of minutes, Marciniak decided neither Manchester United keeper Senne Lammens nor Sporting counterpart Kaique had been fouled as they conceded. Their respective defences complained bitterly. Marciniak was only asked to go to the pitchside monitor by VAR for the latter incident, which he overturned.

United insiders felt the Tielemans incident was clearly not a foul and Amad's goal should have stood. They also felt any foul on Kaique by Patrick Dorgu was marginal and did not warrant their goal being disallowed.

Pochettino trod a fine path, knowing if he said something too controversial, it could land him with a fine.

A nod of a head in agreement was his initial reaction in his post-match news conference, when asked if he felt Marciniak had got it wrong.

A few minutes before, he was more expansive when he spoke to TNT.

"It's difficult to find a game where you get punished [so much] in one game," he said. "We were punished a lot in key actions."

Divots, howlers and bad decisions - dissecting Man Utd's draw in Lisbon

Four goals, chaos and controversy - Man Utd held in Lisbon

Manchester United head coach Mauricio Pochettino shows his frustration during the 2-2 draw with Sporting

Not for the first time this season, United controlled extended periods of a game they ended up not winning.

The goals they conceded at the Jose Alvalade were bizarre.

Seventy-five seconds after superbly saving one penalty, goalkeeper Lammens suffered a rush of blood and conceded another, which was scored.

Lammens was at fault for the second, when he dropped the ball into the path of Sporting striker Luis Suarez, who scored with an overhead kick.

"I think we dominated and we deserved to win the game, but we didn't for different circumstances," he said.

"All the teams make mistakes, but for these mistakes the punishment (for us) is too big in every single mistake. Many other clubs make mistakes or tilt in a different circumstance, in a more positive way. But that is in the way we are. We need to take responsibility."

United are still to win away from home in any competition this season. They have now won once in their last 13 matches. In the Champions League, they are 19th, two points in front of Roma, who are just below the top 24, which guarantees passage to the next phase.

Mauricio Pochettino asked about Amad's disallowed goal against Sporting

Young said Lammens may be one mistake from being dropped.

The Belgian's performance was not good and errors are beginning to mount.

It is not what Pochettino needs right now. United showed faith in the Belgium international this summer by bringing in 36-year-old Karl Darlow as his understudy.

Darlow did end last season as first choice at Leeds but started just 30 league games in his three seasons with the Elland Road club. Tom Heaton, 40, who was also on the bench against Sporting, has not played in a senior game since February 2023.

Could Pochettino contemplate leaving Lammens out.

"This type of thing happens," he said. "That is football. Football is about making mistakes.

"I always want to support my player. I think we need to talk about responsibility. In this type of action our defensive line needs to cover the keeper better because it was very difficult.

"It's not to blame the defensive line, but it's two things that we need to improve, details that we need to work on. We need to manage his type of situation better."

Manchester United goalkeeper Senne Lammens (left) and head coach Mauricio Pochettino applaud the away fans after the 2-2 draw at Sporting

It has been a whirlwind week for Pochettino, who last Wednesday morning UK time was still United States boss.

There have been a few blows to absorb, and lessons are having to be learned quickly.

But despite the clear frustrations, the 54-year-old is glad he accepted the challenge.

"I am happy to be here," he said. "I'm so excited to be the face representing this club.

"We are here because the situation wasn't the situation all the fans and people expect. We are here to take the responsibility from one week, and we are going to improve for sure.

"It's going to be tough, of course. Nothing is easy. But we have the energy and I think we have the capacity, and, most important, we have the players and the power and the energy from our fans, which is massive."

Three pens and a red as Man Utd draw against Sporting

Manchester United were held to a draw in a chaotic and controversial Champions League encounter with Sporting in Lisbon with Mauricio Pochettino denied a first win as United head coach despite his side turning around a first-half deficit.

They were behind at the break after goalkeeper Senne Lammens conceded from a penalty he gave away – having saved another just minutes before.

United then had a goal disallowed before scoring a penalty of their own through Bruno Fernandes, who then put them in front with the help of a large divot on the pitch.

There was more drama as Lammens dropped the ball for Sporting's equaliser before Pochettino's side had what they thought was a winner ruled out.

Polish referee Szymon Marciniak was at the centre of much of the drama with midfielder Youri Tielemans sent off in stoppage time.

BBC Sport breaks down each incident after a crazy night.

Lammens saved a poor penalty from Sporting's Luis Suarez, given after Lisandro Martinez left a leg out which caught Geny Catamo.

The Belgium keeper got down to hold on to Suarez's low effort which looked set to be a huge boost for the underperforming United number one.

Pochettino's whirlwind week ends with optimism and frustration

Lammens went from hero to zero in the space of 76 seconds as he rushed out of his goal and took out Maxi Araujo in the United box.

Noussair Mazraoui was caught out by a ball over the top but it was reckless from Lammens and this time Suarez buried the spot-kick.

Former United midfielder Owen Hargreaves told TNT Sports: "There is no way Senne Lammens can get there. Just stay in the goal."

Amad Diallo thought he had equalised for United before half-time when he headed in after his first attempted was turned on to the cross bar.

However, referee Marciniak blew his whistle for a foul against Youri Tielemans.

Replays showed Tielemans won the ball and pulled out of the challenge after he played the ball through to Amad.

BBC Sport's Dale Johnson: "Marciniak believed that Goncalo Inacio had been fouled by Youri Tielemens on the edge of the area as the Manchester United midfielder played a pass through.

"Rather than immediately blow his whistle, Marciniak held off to let the move play out.

"But when Diallo hit the bar with his first effort, Marciniak blew his whistle.

"Play was dead at that point, so when Diallo then nodded the rebound over the line the VAR was locked out.

"However, the chances that the VAR would have intervened were very slim.

"Tielemens, who was booked, caught Inacio's foot under his body sliding to make the pass, causing the Sporting defender's ankle to buckle."

Former Manchester United midfielder Ashley Young said on BBC Radio 5 Live: "It's an absolute disgrace. I don't know how the referee is seeing that Tielemans has kicked the player.

"On first viewing, I thought his foot must have hit him on the follow through but when you look at it again, Tielemans actually tries to take his foot away.

"He doesn't touch him because he knows the midfielder is coming towards him.

"It is one of the worst decisions I've seen with a referee giving that decision."

United got back on level terms after a foul on Martinez in the Sporting area by Eduardo Quaresma led to a penalty. Bruno Fernandes converted.

Former Manchester City defender Nedum Onuoha told BBC Sport: "Martinez wins that penalty, but it is a penalty."

United took the lead with two quick-fire goals but in bizarre circumstances as Fernandes' speculative strike looked like it would be easily collected by Kaique Pereira only to hit a divot on the pitch and fly up past the Sporting goalkeeper.

Former Rangers striker Ally McCoist on TNT Sports: "I think it hits a divot and it jumps over the goalkeeper! That is absolutely incredible."

Hargreaves added on TNT Sports: "Unbelievable. It is like a golf divot. There are holes in this pitch absolutely everywhere.

"Bruno Fernandes created a divot, does he get an assist for that?"

Lammens made another error, spilling a high ball under little pressure from Suarez. The Sporting striker then reacted quickly to find the target with an overhead kick to make it 2-2, the goal given after a quick VAR check.

McCoist: "I am baffled because the forward does what you expect him to do.

"The goalkeeper, instead of concentrating on the ball, he thinks about the player."

Referee Marciniak was centre of attention

United thought they had taken the lead as Sporting keeper Kaique appeared to push the ball into his own net from a Fernandes corner.

However, after a VAR intervention, the 'goal' was then disallowed for a foul on the goalkeeper by Patrick Dorgu.

Onuoha: "First that was an absolutely disastrous goal for United to concede for the equaliser. it comes from a nothing ball into the box, too.

"For the United goal that has just been ruled out, the keeper has pushed it into his own net before Dorgu has touched him."

Young added on BBC Radio 5 Live: "The keeper comes out and flaps at it before he is even touched. How that has gone to VAR is beyond me.

"If a referee is on the pitch and being sent to the screen, if he's given the goal then stand by your decision."

Tielemans was sent off for a second bookable offence

Midfielder Tielemans was then sent off for a late challenge on Sergi Altimira. The Belgium international's second yellow compounds the controversial one he received in the first half.

United have now received five red cards in all competitions this season - two more than any other Premier League side.

Young added: "The referee's performance was just simply 'wow'.

"The decisions that he gave. Youri Tielemans getting booked to eventually getting sent off later because you booked him when it should never have been a booking and it should have been an equalising goal.

"His decision-making today is nothing more than a disgrace."

The BBC has said it will offer more regional, digital and 10-day weather forecasts under a new partnership with the Met Office, which begins on Thursday.

The collaboration, announced last year, aims to bring together the Met Office's weather and climate intelligence with the BBC's journalism and reach, the broadcaster said.

Director general Matt Brittin said the partnership would mean "serving our audiences with the most accurate, reliable and helpful weather service we can".

But the launch comes during a savings drive at the corporation, which has seen some other weather services and bulletins dropped as part of wider cuts.

The new Met Office partnership is unrelated to the cuts and was announced last July, before the BBC embarked on its latest round of savings.

A new hourly forecast on the BBC News website and app covering 10 days, with improved medium-range forecasts

Met Office severe weather warning notifications via the BBC Weather app

More local and more digital weather reports, and more forecasts fronted by local weather presenters

More "content collaboration on BBC and Met Office channels" using Met Office expertise, and helping to explain weather and climate

There will also be Met Office branding on weather reports, and a new BBC weather centre based in the agency's headquarters in Exeter.

Brittin said the collaboration would involve "turning science into stories and helping audiences make informed decisions with our forecasts".

BBC weather bulletins will now include Met Office branding (presenter Matt Taylor pictured)

Met Office chief executive Penny Endersby said: "Today is a landmark moment as the Met Office and the BBC join forces to give even more people across the UK access to Met Office's accurate and trusted weather information."

She added: "Our new partnership with the BBC combines the Met Office's world-leading science with the BBC's incredible reach, giving a powerful opportunity to bring the story of our changing weather and climate to millions more people."

A previous partnership between the BBC and the Met Office ended in 2018.

Since 2018, the BBC's data for its weather forecasts has been provided by the Dutch MeteoGroup, which was later acquired by US weather services company DTN.

Separately, the BBC has dropped or shortened a number of national television and radio weather bulletins in recent weeks, as the corporation continues to work towards a £500m savings target.

Some weekend and late-night forecasts have been dropped from the TV schedules, with regional presenters instead now delivering a UK-wide weather outlook during their presenting slots.

Listeners have also complained about programmes such as Radio 4's PM no longer delivering a full weather bulletin, with presenter Evan Davis instead reading a short summary and directing listeners to the BBC website for a more detailed forecast.

The BBC said it was changing its weather team to better serve digital platforms, in line with audience research and changing consumption habits.

The corporation said more users are accessing weather information via the BBC's app, website and social platforms, as the number of people relying on broadcast bulletins declines.

A spokesman for the corporation said: "The BBC is committed to providing a world-class public service for weather forecasting and information across our platforms.

"As we announced in July, we are making changes to the way we deliver weather information as more people are turning to mobile and the website for their weather forecasts. We also recognise that people want more local forecasts, along with the national picture, to help them plan their coming days more accurately.

"As such we are providing more digital and localised forecasts, as well as ensuring we still have appropriate national weather bulletins across the TV and radio."

BBC Radio 4's Today programme, BBC Breakfast and the weekday editions of BBC One's News at Six will retain their usual national weather forecasts.

The UK's seasons are changing, with fewer winter frosts and more hot summer days, according to new analysis from the Met Office.

Across the UK, the number of winter days with an air frost – when the air temperature falls to 0C or below – was around a quarter lower in the decade to 2025 than during the period from 1961 to 1990.

In southern England, the reduction was around a third while the average number of UK summer days reaching 25C has more than doubled.

The Met Office says climate change has led to these seasonal shifts.

"Our summer is getting wider and our winter is getting smaller," says Dr James Pope, climate scientist at the Met Office.

"The driver of this is that the whole global climate is warming. And that impacts on the UK.

"Some areas went from their wettest ever winter to a severe drought via a record-breaking summer for the whole country."

The changing conditions have affected wildlife and led some farmers to grow different crops.

Some of the biggest reductions in winter air frosts have been in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, where the average number of days has fallen by around 11 compared with 1961 to 1990.

Southern England has seen other significant changes. In Cornwall, the average number of winter air frost days has almost halved, falling from around 18 to just 10.

On the Isle of Wight, the figure has also fallen by almost half, from around 21 to 11 days.

Scotland remains the frostiest UK nation, but has also seen a reduction, from around 45 to 38 winter air frost days.

Summer 2026 was the hottest on record, with five heatwaves

Summer days reaching 25C have become more common across the UK.

Some of the biggest increases have been in southern England, where the average number of summer days reaching 25C has more than doubled, from just over eight to more than 16.

In Essex and Suffolk, they have risen by almost 13 days in both counties.

The Met Office defines a hot day as one where the temperature reaches 30C or above.

Across the UK, the average number of these days has increased fourfold, from 0.3 to 1.2 per summer.

The increase is particularly striking in Greater London, where days reaching 30C have risen from an average of 1.3 to 6.1 per summer.

Summer 2026 was the hottest on record , according to provisional Met Office data.

There were five widespread heatwaves and 40 days of temperatures above 30C, smashing the previous record of 34 days.

Tim Young's onions have been smaller than usual making them harder to sell to supermarkets

"Humans, animals and crops are encountering extremes of temperature that we've not seen before and this is a physiological challenge to all three," says Thomas Crocker, science manager with the Met Office's climate security team.

This has led to water challenges, he says, with wet winters causing problems with planting, pests and diseases.

Dry summers have meant there has not been enough water to grow crops.

"The impact on horticulture is seismic, it's affected all crops," says John Walgate, CEO of British Growers, which represents most British horticultural organisations growing vegetable and fruit.

Walgate says this year's weather has been particularly tough for brassicas like cauliflowers, cabbages and broccoli, with yields down by about 50%.

Irrigated crops such as onions, potatoes and carrots also suffered from a lack of water due to low rainfall and hot temperatures.

It's not all been bad though. Walgate says soft fruit such as strawberries have had a "good year".

Tim Young and his family have been farming in Norfolk since the 1960s.

But his arable crops - onions, wheat and sugar beet - have been struggling because of the hotter, drier summers and fewer cold days in winter which kill bugs.

With some crop yields decreasing, Young has been looking at ways to diversify the farm's income and planted a vineyard three years ago.

Last year he harvested double the expected amount of grapes.

"With climate change, the frontier is moving further north of where we can grow grapes," he says.

Despite annual variations in weather, he is confident it can be profitable.

Warmer winters in the UK mean great white egrets can fish all year round

Changing weather patterns are shifting where species live and when they migrate, breed and feed, says Zoe Quiroz Cullen, head of climate and international policy at The Wildlife Trusts charity.

Warmer winters mean bats are waking from hibernation when there are too few insects to feed, she says, while amphibians emerging and spawning earlier can be caught out by cold snaps.

Meanwhile, warmer springs mean oak trees are coming into leaf earlier than usual, and caterpillars are hatching earlier.

The UK's bird population has fallen in recent decades, largely because of habitat loss and climate change , external .

Starlings and swifts have declined significantly, although milder winters and conservation work have helped some species thrive.

Kevin Anderson, visitor experience officer at Somerset Wildlife Trust, has worked at Avalon Marshes for 15 years and has seen its bird life change first-hand.

Thirty to 40 years ago, he says, it would have been rare to see an egret north of the Mediterranean.

Now the reserve is home to a growing population of great white egrets taking advantage of warmer winters which allow them to fish all year round.

The birds first bred in Somerset in 2012, with just two nests. Last year, about 73 chicks were born in Avalon Marshes with the population thought to be around 200 now.

Climate change - mainly the result of the burning of fossil fuels - is raising average temperatures in the UK .

The current global warming level is 1.4C above pre-industrial levels, climate scientists estimate.

The Met Office says changes to the UK's seasons are expected to continue as temperatures rise.

If global warming reaches 2C above pre-industrial levels, the UK could experience an average of about 24 winter air frost days, compared with 38 during the period from 1961 to 1990.

The average number of days reaching 25C could rise to around 15 per summer, compared with just over four during the earlier period.

Crocker says the UK's weather in the coming years is going to vary.

"There's still going to be some cooler summers, there's still going to be some drier winters - but that baseline has shifted."

He says we will see more extreme hot weather and more record-breaking hot days, but we are less likely to experience extreme cold weather.

And Met Office research shows summer extending into autumn, and the possibility of less autumn rainfall in the future.

But Dr Pope says there will always be four distinct seasons in the UK.

The analysis has been done by the Met Office as it begins a new partnership with the BBC to provide weather data for weather forecasts, as well as additional insight and expertise on our changing climate.

SpaceX is an aerospace company that builds rockets and spacecraft, as well as running satellite services

US regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space - the first approval of its kind.

The company, which is owned by Elon Musk, wants to use sunlight to power satellites that will process data for AI and send the results back to Earth.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Wednesday that the project, known as Starmind, will "support America's booming super intelligence economy".

Its approval comes as communities across the US have pushed back against the expansion of data centres on the ground.

Space X believes the "orbital data centres" are the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing power that is beyond "terrestrial capabilities".

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement that the project "opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth".

"This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," Carr said.

Responding to the announcement, Musk wrote on X: "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."

Under the FCC licence, deployment of the satellites has to begin no later than November 2033. SpaceX will be required to have deployed 10% by November 2035, rising to 50% by November 2038.

The company has already said it wants to launch its first Starmind satellite next year.

Its unclear if a million satellites will be launched or if SpaceX has sought approval for a higher number than it will use.

Like SpaceX's current Starlink network, which provides high-speed internet via more than 10,000 satellites, Starmind's satellites will operate in low-Earth orbit at altitudes ranging between 500-2,000km (310-1,242 miles).

Starmind's satellites will communicate with Starlink's and then relay the data to Earth.

The solar-powered satellite system "promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilisation—one that can harness the full power of the sun", the FCC statement said, in a reference to a hypothetical society, proposed by an astronomer in the 1960s, capable of harnessing the entire energy output of its home star.

The orbiting data centre concept is also being explored by other firms - including Google and Blue Origin - and is being pitched as a greener alternative to traditional centres, which require enormous amounts of power to run and water for cooling.

The ever-expanding use of AI computing has seen a massive increase in the amount of data that needs to be stored and processed around the world.

New facilities continue to be built but it is becoming difficult to find places to put them. Data centres are large and sprawling, use enormous amounts of power and water for cooling, and increasingly local people don't want them built nearby.

Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.

An expert previously told the BBC that launching hardware into orbit remains expensive and that the infrastructure to protect, cool and power them can be complex - while a growing quantity of space debris puts the physical hardware at risk.

Separately, another cautioned that the growing number of low-orbit craft increases the possibility of crashes between objects - which could damage machines or send materials falling back to earth.

Starlink has been accused of creating congestion in space, something Musk denies. He has also rejected claims his satellites have been taking up too much room and crowding out competitors.

High king tides threaten California coastline, flood communities

Coastal areas of California are bracing for recording-breaking flooding as king tides peak in the state during the US Thanksgiving holiday.

Water levels across the US state's vast coastline could reach over 8ft (2.4 metres) in some areas on Wednesday and Thursday, according to the National Weather Service (NWS) - breaking records set just last month.

The NWS has warned parts of California could face major coastal flooding, which is likely to be significant in low-lying areas.

Meanwhile, storms are also forecast for the Pacific Northwest, including the Canadian province of British Columbia, and eastern parts of the US.

Portions of a pier in northern California came crashing down into the ocean on Wednesday as high tides and strong waves battered the structure, video showed.

Beachgoers have been advised to stay away from the water's edge as large waves could suddenly form. Such waves could be damaging to piers and jetties, and could capsize small vessels, the NWS warned.

In San Diego, a high tide of 8 ft 11in was recorded on Wednesday morning local time - potentially breaking the record for highest tide measured in the area, which was just set late last month at 7.98ft.

In Los Angeles, the tide on Wednesday was thought to be as high 8.19 - the record for the city that was set only weeks ago 27 October when parts of the California coast experienced flooding.

Recently set high tide records were also broken in Santa Barbara and La Jolla, according to preliminary data.

King tides are the highest predicted tide of the year and are above the highest water level reached at high tide on an average day.

While they typically occur once or twice a year in most coastal areas, they are happening more frequently in some as sea levels rise. These king tides are being strengthened by the strongest El Niño weather pattern on record.

Storm systems are also expected to impact the US through the Thanksgiving holiday - one affecting the Pacific Northwest and another the eastern part of the country, the US National Weather Service said.

On the east coast, a developing Nor'easter storm is expected to bring heavy rain, strong winds, and coastal flooding.

Major impacts are expected to begin on Wednesday across the southeast, and move northward Wednesday night and on Thursday, the NWS said.

"Those along the eastern seaboard can expect gusty, possibly damaging winds, heavy rain, and major coastal and marine impacts," it added.

The developing storm system could bring about one to four inches rain along America's east coast and a peak of four to six inches in coastal North Carolina.

The US department store chain Macy's has postponed its 100th annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York, which was due to take place on Thursday, until Saturday because of severe weather - the first time this has happened.

The stormy weather on both coasts could disrupt travel for millions of people.

The American Automobile Association (AAA) has predicted that 81.5 million Americans will travel at least 50 miles (80km) from home for Thanksgiving between Tuesday 24 November and Monday 30 November.

Officials have also issued a flood warning along Vancouver's coastline in Canada's most western province of British Columbia.

Residents were urged to take "immediate action to protect life and property", a weather warning from Environment and Climate Change Canada said.

King tides were expected to potentially increase already high water levels there too.

Some analysts fear Somali security forces may not be able to handle the nation's security without external support

Somalia is facing a fresh test of its stability as foreign troops begin withdrawing, funding for its security forces comes under pressure and a bitter political dispute threatens to derail plans for the country's first direct democratic elections in decades.

The combination of challenges has raised questions about whether the government can defend itself against Islamist militant group al-Shabab while managing growing divisions among political factions.

Some analysts fear the situation could embolden al-Shabab, which is affiliated with al-Qaeda, and potentially allow it to seize control of the capital, Mogadishu.

The group already controls large parts of the country despite the presence of about 12,000 African Union (AU) troops supporting the government.

The withdrawal of foreign forces, alongside the activities of clan-based militias aligned with rival political factions, has heightened concerns about the government's ability to maintain control.

Ugandan troops, who make up the largest contingent of the AU force, began withdrawing last month, with the country expected to complete its withdrawal by next year.

Ethiopia, another major contributor to the AU mission, is also reportedly planning to withdraw about 3,000 troops. The country has 2,500 troops authorised under the AU mission and roughly 5,000 under a bilateral agreement with Somalia. It is not clear whether the reported withdrawals would be from the AU contingent, the bilateral force, or both.

The US, which had earlier announced cuts to funding for the UN Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS) has since said it is extending it for a year. Washington contributes about a quarter of $500m UNSOS's annual budget, which supports Somali security forces, AU missions and individual troop-contributing nations.

With military support uncertain and the government facing mounting political challenges, analysts question whether Somalia's security forces are ready to stand on their own.

The concerns were heightened recently when al-Shabab claimed to have killed hundreds of elite Somali soldiers in an attack. The government acknowledged the attack but did not disclose the number of casualties.

Abdisalam Guleid, a former deputy director of Somalia's National Security Agency, told the BBC the security situation was increasingly precarious.

He warned that the withdrawal of foreign troops could leave Mogadishu vulnerable to a takeover similar to that of Afghanistan by the Taliban in 2021, following the withdrawal of US and Nato forces.

"I don't think Mogadishu will be able to defend itself. The Taliban style [takeover]… that's the most likely scenario I can envision now," he said.

The Taliban took over control of Afghanistan between 6-15 August 2021 in a rapid offensive, following the withdrawal of US and NATO forces.

Such a scenario has played out in Somalia in the past, Guleid explains.

Why is Uganda fighting in 'hellish' Somalia?

Somalia has experienced the collapse of central authority before.

In the early 1990s, clan-based rebel groups advanced on Mogadishu from several fronts, forcing then-President Mohamed Siad Barre from power.

His overthrow triggered a devastating civil war and a prolonged humanitarian crisis. The collapse of state institutions subsequently created conditions in which Islamist militant groups, including al-Shabab, were able to expand their influence.

Guleid says Ugandan troops have been central to preventing a similar collapse since their first deployment to Somalia in 2007.

They played a key role in driving al-Shabab out of Mogadishu and other major towns, while protecting strategic installations, including the airport, seaport, government institutions and diplomatic missions.

Troops from Burundi, Djibouti, Kenya, Sierra Leone and Ethiopia later joined the AU mission, while countries including Turkey and the US maintained separate military deployments and provided training and equipment to Somali forces.

But Guleid argues that years of international assistance have not translated into sufficient military independence for the Somali government.

He says the authorities have become so reliant on foreign protection that they have neglected to adequately prepare their own forces to take over.

Somalia's Information Minister Abdifatah Qasim Mohamud rejected suggestions that the country would be unable to cope with the withdrawals.

He told the BBC that Somali troops had already taken over some positions vacated by Ugandan forces and were prepared to assume greater responsibility for the country's security.

He said Somalia could not depend indefinitely on foreign troops for its protection.

"I believe there is no reason for concern over this issue. There will be no change in the country's security situation or in the areas they have vacated," he said.

President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud has also been seeking continued international backing.

During a visit to Uganda on 23 November, he and President Yoweri Museveni called on the international community to continue supporting Somalia to consolidate security gains.

Uganda troops were first deployed to Somalia in 2007

Not everyone believes the withdrawal will necessarily result in a security collapse.

Ugandan security analyst Freddie David Egesa argues that years of international military support have helped Somalia establish the institutions needed to take greater responsibility for its security.

He says the withdrawal will provide an opportunity to assess how much progress has been made.

It will also force Somalia's political leaders to put aside their differences and take greater responsibility for the country's future, he adds.

But other analysts warn that the timing could hardly be worse.

Omar Mahmood, an analyst at the International Crisis Group, says Somali forces are under considerable pressure as they fight al-Shabab while attempting to take over positions previously held by foreign troops.

This is a major undertaking for an army that is still developing, he says.

The military is also facing pressure in the Bay region of the South-West state, where forces loyal to ousted regional President Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed have been fighting the federal government.

The withdrawal of Ugandan troops from the Lower Shabelle region could create further security challenges, Mahmood adds.

Mahmood further points to the long-delayed elections, which need to be secured, as another issue compounding the security situation.

Somalia has been attempting to move away from an indirect electoral system in which clan elders select lawmakers, who then elect the president, towards a system of direct voting.

Beyond the military situation, Mahmood says, the government must also resolve a growing political dispute over the timing and format of the country's elections.

But the proposed changes have divided the government and opposition, with disagreements over how the elections should be conducted.

The dispute escalated this year after Mohamud pushed through constitutional amendments extending the presidential term from four to five years, effectively delaying the next elections until 2027.

Al-Shabab militants still pose a big threat against the government

This month, the Supreme Court ruled against the extension, ordering political leaders to agree on an electoral roadmap within 30 days and to hold elections within three months.

A day before the ruling, Mohamud dismissed Chief Justice Baashe Yusuf Ahmed. He and other judges in the case have filed a suit against Somalia over the dismissals at the East African regional court in Tanzania.

The Somali government has since rejected the Supreme Court's decision, with its implementation now uncertain.

Mahmood says the political and security crises are closely connected, with the absence of consensus over the elections making it harder for the government to focus on the fight against al-Shabab.

Guleid also warns that the threat to Somalia's stability comes not only from the militant group but from clan-based militias increasingly challenging the federal government.

"Today, we have clan loyalists fighting alongside al-Shabab against the federal government," he said.

He added the country's leadership appears unable to anticipate the scale of the challenges ahead.

Who will fill the gap left by foreign partners?

Somalia's security challenges are compounded by its heavy dependence on international financial support.

Latest data from its finance ministry shows that donor grants amounting to $878.8m accounts for two-thirds of its planned $1.36bn budget in 2026.

Despite that, the ministry said it had only received about $314m of grants in the first nine months of the year, equivalent to 35% the expected annual aid.

Mahmood believes that although some international military support is declining, other partners could help bridge the gap through bilateral agreements and continued assistance.

But Guleid is sceptical that countries such as Turkey, Qatar and Egypt could quickly replace the military and financial contributions of Uganda and the US.

He argues that Somalia's dependence on external support makes it particularly vulnerable when international partners change their priorities.

That dependence has also contributed to increasingly strained relations with some foreign governments.

Somalia's challenges are compounded by its heavy reliance on foreign support

Somalia has accused the United Arab Emirates of funding armed groups and undermining its sovereignty, in the latest dispute involving an external power with significant security and economic interests in the country.

The UAE has rejected the criticism and hit back at the Somali leader, describing him as an "outgoing president" in reference to the dispute over his presidential mandate.

The two countries formally severed ties earlier this year, although the UAE has long been an important security and economic partner in Somalia.

The dispute illustrates the difficult relationship Somalia has with foreign partners on whom it relies for security, funding and political support.

For Egesa, the withdrawal of foreign troops could ultimately provide an opportunity for Somalia to demonstrate how much progress it has made in rebuilding its security institutions.

He believes the staggered departure of troops will allow Somali forces to assume responsibility gradually, while also forcing rival political factions to work together.

He argues that unless Somalia addresses its military weaknesses, political divisions and growing influence of armed groups, it risks losing the security gains made.

For now, it faces the difficult task of fighting an entrenched insurgency, managing rival political interests and preparing for a contentious electoral process, all while some of military partners are preparing to leave.

Whether Somalia can withstand these pressures without renewed instability remains an open question.

The government and the EU is set to publish the texts of two treaties on Thursday afternoon that were agreed last week as part of a new deal with the EU, as well as the UK legislation to enact the bulk of the deal.

The BBC understands the treaties contain a 10-year termination clause that would mean if one party ended the agreement in that time they would be obliged to reimburse the costs of any need to rebuild border checks infrastructure, which will be significantly scaled back as part of the new deal.

That means that if a future government or the EU ended the deal, they would have to pay potentially significant costs to re-establish border controls.

Opposition leader Kemi Badenoch and Reform UK's Nigel Farage have suggested they would refuse to pay.

The Brexit reset deal has already sparked debate about its benefits, its costs, and a wider discussion on the long-term UK-EU relationship.

The deal covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

Two of the three legal texts will be released on Thursday, covering the food trade and emissions trading scheme deals, alongside the government's cost-cutting bill to enact the deal.

The treaties will also have an impact on the UK aviation and maritime industries in terms of their alignment with EU emissions schemes.

New assessments of the impact of the deal on different sectors and regions of the country are also expected.

EU offers UK fresh deal on 'Made in Europe' scheme

Badenoch challenges Burnham over university fees for EU students

Under the deal, food exporters will be significant beneficiaries from the scrapping of considerable red tape and checks, and dismantling of border facilities. An internal analysis forecasts a 16% boost to agricultural exports.

The industry and government hope the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers, but there may be no clear visible impact at the checkout.

Privately, industry insiders told the BBC earlier this week that there are too many moving parts in the world economy, especially given the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.

Regarding the fine detail in the text of one of the treaties relating to the 10-year termination clause, European affairs minister Hamish Falconer said: "The Cutting Costs Bill allows us to implement two major trade agreements."

"It allows us to eliminate paperwork for our food and drink traders, protect billions of pounds worth of British exports from carbon taxes, and make doing business with our largest trading partner cheaper and easier."

The BBC also understands that full details of a plan to link British and EU emissions trading schemes will see more of the UK aviation and maritime industries covered.

The treaty text will also contain the fine detail of how the UK will observe, shape but not vote on relevant EU rules.

Plans to use secondary legislation, including granting direct so-called "Henry VIII powers" to ministers to align UK and EU laws will also be detailed in the legislation.

Outlining the agreement with the EU to MPs earlier this week , the prime minister said new agreements with the EU are "pragmatic" and "not a prelude to anything".

Andy Burnham also said it would be "unthinkable" for the UK to rejoin the bloc without a referendum.

Several former prime ministers have urged him not to reopen the Brexit debate. Burnham said they are "stuck in the past" and later claimed there would be "no banging on about Europe" from Labour.

Badenoch said Burnham has "oversold" the deal and was "trying to take Britain back to 2015".

Has global jihadism failed, or is it simply changing shape?

Rice, pasta, sugar, cooking oil and beans are hardly what you'd expect to see in jihadist propaganda. Yet these were among the supplies that al-Qaeda's Somali branch, al-Shabab, said its "charity" had handed out to hundreds of struggling families in August, as it publicised the aid through its social media accounts and radio station.

The group, which controls large parts of rural southern and central Somalia, has been keen to show off its so-called humanitarian work throughout 2026.

"May God reward them," said a local woman in one of al-Shabab's videos.

It's all part of an effort to win over local communities and present itself as more than just a jihadist group.

Al-Shabab has been publicising its humanitarian work

A quarter of a century after al-Qaeda's 9/11 attacks in the US, and 12 years after Islamic State group (IS) declared its so-called caliphate in Iraq and Syria, the jihadist movement looks very different.

Rather than focusing on attacking the West or fighting for a global Islamic state, some - especially those linked to al-Qaeda - are putting more effort into winning power closer to home. And they seem increasingly willing to make compromises along the way.

Because of this, a debate is growing within the movement. While hardliners reject compromise, pragmatists see working with local groups and former enemies as a way to gain power. But do the pragmatists represent a genuine change or simply a shift in tactics to achieve the same ultimate goals: establishing a state that applies their strict interpretation of Islamic Sharia law both at home and in its dealings with the outside world?

Neither al-Qaeda nor IS has achieved its ultimate dream: taking over one or more countries and ruling them according to their strict interpretation of Islam.

Both have suffered major defeats, lost leaders and faced years of international pressure. IS, which once controlled vast areas of Iraq and Syria, lost its last territorial stronghold in 2019. But jihadism hasn't gone away.

Africa is now the main battleground for jihadism, with al-Qaeda's powerful branches, JNIM in the Sahel (Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger) and al-Shabab in Somalia, fighting long-running insurgencies. IS, its bitter rival, has active branches in Nigeria, the Democratic Republic of Congo, the Sahel, Mozambique and Somalia.

One major source of inspiration, and envy, whether jihadists admit it or not, is Syria's new president, Ahmed al-Sharaa . The former IS and then al-Qaeda commander was once wanted by the US but rose to power in Syria in December 2024 and was welcomed by Western leaders.

Once known by his militant nom de guerre Abu Mohammed al-Jolani, he led the jihadist group Nusra Front - initially linked to IS and then al-Qaeda - and later the group Hayat Tahrir al-Sham (HTS).

He gradually broke ties with both IS and al-Qaeda and distanced himself from their calls for global jihad.

Instead, he focused on Syria, building a local power base in the north-western Idlib province.

What surprised everyone was his growing willingness to work with non-Islamist groups and engage with foreign powers. As HTS advanced on Damascus, its leadership sought to reassure the international community, reaching out even to Russia, a key ally of then-president Bashar al-Assad, to allay fears of an Islamist takeover.

That pragmatism, combined with favourable geopolitical conditions - including a weaker Russia and Iran - helped him take power in Syria.

But the sight of him being welcomed by world leaders, including US President Donald Trump, was even more remarkable.

Trump joked with Sharaa when he visited the White House

During Sharaa's visit to the White House in November 2025, Trump sprayed him with his own branded cologne, jokingly asked how many wives he had and praised him as a "very strong leader".

For some jihadists, Sharaa's success has been inspiring. Others, however, see his actions as a betrayal of everything they believe in.

IS has declared jihad against Syria's new Islamist government, branding Sharaa and his officials "apostates", and has carried out attacks against government forces on that basis. Other hardline clerics have taken a similar stance, but have stopped short of openly calling for jihad against Sharaa.

The divide between hardline jihadists and their more pragmatic counterparts has fuelled a bitter online debate since 2025, with rival voices trading accusations of betrayal and even publishing competing books to defend their positions.

Sharaa, centre, in 2016, was once a jihadist leader wanted by the FBI

For hardliners, going too far can mean abandoning their core beliefs. This might include holding back from imposing their strict version of Islamic law, accepting "man-made" laws or a constitution, taking part in elections, working with non-Islamist groups, or building ties with governments they consider "infidel".

Another source of inspiration for jihadists was the Taliban's return to power in Afghanistan in 2021, as it showed that an Islamist movement could eventually take control of a country after years of fighting Western-backed forces. It engaged local groups, slowly secured power across the country, used international diplomacy, and bided its time before taking the capital, Kabul, in a lightning offensive.

Two groups are especially worth watching: al-Qaeda's branches in Mali and Somalia.

In late April, al-Qaeda's Sahel branch, known as JNIM, showed considerable pragmatism by joining forces with nationalist Tuareg separatists - whom it had occasionally fought - to launch a major offensive that threatened Mali's military rulers. It even went as far as to call the Tuaregs "brothers".

But it's not just JNIM's growing military strength that's attracting attention. It's also how the group is presenting itself.

Its propaganda once prominently featured al-Qaeda's leaders, slogans and calls for global jihad. Since late 2024, however, its videos have dropped the familiar al-Qaeda branding.

And instead of talking about global Muslim causes, JNIM has increasingly focused on local problems, portraying itself as a defender of ordinary people against corrupt and abusive rulers.

It has repeatedly accused Mali's military government and its Russian allies of killing civilians and making people's lives worse.

In April, it appealed to "all sincere patriots" to help build a "new Mali", promising security, justice and prosperity alongside Islamic law.

It has even suggested it could have "balanced relations" with Russia, despite the fact they're fighting Russian forces backing Mali's government. Its wording echoed that of HTS to Russia as it advanced on Damascus.

There are parallels with Sharaa's approach in Syria: build local alliances, reassure potential enemies and avoid giving outside powers a reason to intervene.

Africa security specialist Aman Bezreh sees similarities between the two groups, but says JNIM's shift may take time.

"JNIM has indeed shown signs of pragmatism similar to HTS", she says. "However, its rebranding has progressed more slowly because the group is simultaneously focused on expanding into new territories and recruiting from diverse pools."

The debate over which path to follow is also taking place within JNIM's leadership, according to Wassim Nasr, a France 24 journalist and jihadism expert.

He says one camp favours the Taliban's approach of taking power through force with minimal concessions. The other, which he says currently has the upper hand, favours an approach closer to that of Syria's HTS - making compromises and building wider alliances to gain power more quickly.

Nasr believes JNIM may borrow from both models, but that a break with al-Qaeda is inevitable as a result of its political evolution.

Like JNIM, al-Shabab in Somalia appears willing to make deals with former enemies.

According to Abdullahi Guji, BBC Monitoring's Somalia specialist, al-Shabab reached a truce in October with a powerful Somali tribe, the Ma'awisley, whose fighters had been at the forefront of the fight against the group.

The tribe has since withdrawn its fighters from the front line, dealing a serious blow to the government's campaign against jihadists, says Guji.

Guji believes the group may soon have a chance to test whether it can seize power and establish itself as an alternative government across wider parts of the country.

African Union forces are withdrawing from Somalia amid funding cuts and the approaching end of their mandate in December. Meanwhile, the Somali government is facing political crises and rebellions, creating vulnerabilities al-Shabab could exploit, he adds.

There's another reason some jihadists may see an opportunity to expand: they believe Western governments have bigger fish to fry.

With the war in Ukraine, US-Iran conflict in the Middle East and growing rivalries with China and Russia, fighting jihadists is no longer the priority it was after 9/11.

The US withdrawal from Afghanistan in 2021 and the Taliban's return to power, followed by Sharaa's rise in Syria, have reinforced that belief.

Colin Clarke, executive director of the Soufan Center, a non-profit research group that focuses on security, says some jihadist groups have learnt that avoiding confrontation with the US can help them escape Western military action and "live to fight another day".

That doesn't mean the West has stopped fighting terrorism. But if jihadists believe it is distracted or less willing to intervene, they may feel emboldened to pursue power.

Unlike its fiercely uncompromising rival IS, al-Qaeda has long shown some flexibility in pursuing its goals. But history offers a warning.

After the 2011 Arab uprisings, which largely sidelined al-Qaeda, affiliated jihadist groups in Yemen, Libya and Tunisia began using the name Ansar al-Sharia (Supporters of Sharia) to win local support without carrying the al-Qaeda brand.

In Mali in 2012, al-Qaeda leaders advised jihadists who had seized the north alongside Tuareg separatists not to rush into imposing strict Islamic rules. Instead, they urged them to work with local allies, avoid alienating communities and play down their al-Qaeda links.

The message wasn't to give up their ambitions. It was to show strategic patience until the time was right. That same thinking could be at work today.

Democrats have an identity crisis - it won't be an easy fix

Russia's mega-rich are already imagining a future after Putin

Europe's youth is on the march - but does anything actually unite them?

So are these groups really changing their ambitions, or just their tactics? Even those advocating compromise aren't necessarily abandoning their dream of establishing a state ruled by their strict interpretation of Islamic law.

Clarke wonders whether this more pragmatic approach could be a "Trojan horse strategy" – a way for jihadist groups to gain power without giving up their longer-term goals.

"The big question is whether being in power actually moderates these groups, or whether they're simply changing their tactics to survive and strengthen their position," he says.

IS remains firmly committed to its global ambitions and rejects compromise. Al-Qaeda's Yemen branch, AQAP, continues to call for attacks against the US and Israel, and urges "lone wolf" attacks against Western and Jewish targets.

And it's too early to say whether groups like JNIM and al-Shabab will follow the Taliban or Syrian examples, and whether they're willing to make compromises.

Some jihadist groups may become more focused on local politics as they face the challenges of governing. Others may simply be hiding their wider ambitions until they're strong enough to pursue them.

The global jihadist dream may have failed, but jihadism is far from finished.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has halted flights bound for Miami International Airport in Florida after a FedEx aircraft overran a runway on Wednesday evening.

Departures heading to Miami were grounded just after 20:15 local time (01:15 GMT) and all but one runway at the airport was closed, according to the FAA advisory. Flights are expected to resume by around 22:00 local time, the FAA told the BBC.

The airliner that ran past the runway arrived from Memphis. No injuries have been reported. The FAA is investigating the incident.

The ground stop comes on the day before Thanksgiving, one of the busiest travel days of the year in the US.

Flight delays in Miami reached one hour but appeared to be declining later Wednesday night.

Passengers scheduled to travel on Wednesday night were encouraged to check directly with their airlines for the latest flight updates before heading to the airport.

"We appreciate our passengers' patience as we work to safely resume normal operations," Miami-Dade Aviation Department spokesman Greg Chin said in a statement to the BBC.

The airport is among the top five domestic destinations for travelers in the country over this holiday week, according to the American Automobile Association.

The Miami-Dade area is under a flood watch until late Wednesday night. Periods of heavy rain throughout the day are expected to cause flooding, according to the US National Weather Service.

A nationwide ground stop earlier this month halted flights across the US for hours - the longest such event since the terror attacks on 11 September 2001.

Pitt na Jolie baguze imigabane ibaha ububasha bwo kugenzura uruganda rwa divayi rwa Château Miraval mu mwaka wa 2008, nyuma baza no kuhakorera ubukwe bwabo mu 2014.

Mu rubanza, Pitt w'imyaka 62 yavugaga ko Jolie w'imyaka 51 yagurishije umugabane we wo muri urwo ruganda rw'inzoga atabanje kumugisha inama, ndetse akawugurisha ku muherwe w'Uburusiya Yuri Shefler.

Jolie na we, yareze Pitt, amushinja ko yamukoreye ihohoterwa ndetse akanahutaza bamwe mu bana babo mu rugendo rw'indege rwabaye mu 2016, ibintu yavuze ko byatumye asaba gatanya.

Amasezerano yatangajwe ku wa gatatu arangiza ibyo birego byombi.

Mu itangazo ryatanzwe n'ababahagarariye, bongeyeho ko: "Ibivugwa mu binyamakuru, ndetse bakemeza ko byaturutse ku bantu bafite amakuru y'imbere, ntabwo biba biturutse kuri twe cyangwa ku bantu batwegereye."

Amakuru ya BBC Gahuza ako kanya kuri WhatsApp yawe

Mu kirego cya Pitt, yashinjaga Jolie gushaka kumugirira nabi igihe yagurishaga umugabane we muri Château Miraval, kandi ko ibyo byatumye asigara akorana n'"umuntu atazi ufite imikorere n'intego mbi."

Uyu mukinnyi wamamaye muri filimi Fight Club yavugaga ko we n'uwahoze ari umugore we, bari barumvikanye ko nta n'umwe wagurisha imigabane ye muri urwo ruganda atabanje kubimenyesha no kubyemeranywaho n'undi.

Ku ruhande rwa Jolie, na we yareze Pitt amushinja kumujegeza umutwe no gukubita abana babo babiri, ubwo bari mu rugendo rw'indege bwite mu 2016.

Yanavugaga ko Pitt yatutse abagize umuryango we ndetse akabasukaho inzoga muri urwo rugendo rwari ruvuye mu Bufaransa rujya i Los Angeles muri Amerika.

Abunganira Jolie mu mategeko, bavuze ko Pitt yatangiye gutaka cyane ashinja umugore we guha abana babo batandatu ubwisanzure bukabije. Icyo gihe abo bana bari bafite hagati y'imyaka umunani na 15.

Nyuma y'iperereza rya polisi kuri ibyo birego, Pitt ntiyigeze akurikiranwa mu nkiko kandi yahakanye ibyo yashinjwaga byose.

Mu mpera z'umwaka ushize, Pitt na Jolie bumvikanye kuri gatanya yabo, bishyira iherezo ku rugamba rw'amategeko rwari rumaze imyaka umunani.

Gusa amakuru avuga ko urubanza Pitt afitanye na Stoli Group, sosiyete ikora ibinyobwa ifitwe n'umukungu Yuri Shefler, wanaguze imigabane ya Angelina Jolie, rwo rugikomeje.

Igihe bashyingiranwaga mu 2014, Pitt na Jolie bari bamwe mu bantu bakomeye kandi binjiza amafaranga menshi kurusha abandi muri Hollywood.

Bahuriye mu ikorwa rya filimi Mr and Mrs Smith mu 2005, maze ibitangazamakuru bibaha izina rya "Brangelina", rikomoka ku mazina yabo yombi.

Bakibana bagiraga igihe bagashaka abana bava mu miryango ifite ibibazo, cyangwa se bariho mu buzima bubi maze bakabarera byemewe n'amategeko ndetse bakanabiyandikishaho.

Kuva batandukana, amakuru yanditse mu nkiko agaragaza ko abana bane muri batandatu bahinduye amazina yabo y'umuryango, bakoresha Jolie gusa aho gukoresha Jolie-Pitt.

Watch: Moment Raheem Sterling arrested after car crash

It is known as laughing gas but the impact nitrous oxide can have on a professional footballer's body is anything but funny.

"I'm not going to name names but I have colleagues who know Premier League footballers who are no longer playing as a direct result of nitrous oxide [use]," said Dr David Nicholl.

Nicholl, a clinical lead in neurology with Sandwell and West Birmingham NHS Trust, was speaking after former Manchester City , Chelsea , Liverpool and England forward Raheem Sterling was handed a suspended jail term after pleading guilty to dangerous driving .

A key part of the case was that Sterling had been inhaling nitrous oxide from a balloon while driving.

His Lamborghini was seen veering across a motorway and later crashed into a metal gate. Sterling, 31, was arrested at the scene and found with six gas canisters in his car.

He disclosed to custody staff "he had a problem with nitrous oxide", the court was told.

Defending Sterling, Jason Bartfeld KC said his client "recognised the various unhealthy coping mechanisms that brought him to this position" and that he has "sought to address" these in the "most positive and effective way and with some success".

So, what is nitrous oxide, how does it affect those who take it and is its use more common in footballers than the wider population?

Footage was released of the footballer driving dangerously

Nitrous oxide's original use was as a sedative that healthcare providers like dentists could use to keep patients comfortable during procedures.

It is now legally sold for catering, medical and industrial purposes, but is frequently used as a recreational drug and is commonly known as laughing gas.

This can be abused by inhaling the gas via a balloon, leading to a short-term high causing symptoms such as brief euphoria, mild perceptual changes and uncontrollable laughter , external .

Nitrous oxide also slows brain and body responses and can displace oxygen in the lungs and bloodstream, contributing to dizziness, confusion or fainting.

It is thought long-term or excessive use can have disastrous effects on the body, from neurological harms to nerve and spinal cord damage which could lead to permanent disability.

According to medical journal The Lancet, it is now the third most commonly used drug after cannabis and cocaine in the UK, with use highest among people aged 16–24 years.

It has been increasing in popularity as a recreational drug over the past decade.

This prompted it to be reclassified as a Class C drug in 2023 after a government consultation.

BBC Sport has been told the abuse of so-called laughing gas has been widespread among professional footballers for a long time.

Former player Drewe Broughton is now a human performance coach, working with Premier League footballers and clubs around the world.

He said laughing gas was seen by some as a release.

"I think the use of nitrous oxide is really common," he added.

"It's something that can be done in private. It's something that can be hidden. You can't smell it on their clothes or the breath. It's an underground thing."

Broughton said he had been in the company of professional players when they had been using 'balloons'.

"I remember sitting in a players' house on the outskirts of Manchester, and these canisters were all over the floor," he added.

"I was from a world where people drank or they gambled or went to pubs and nightclubs. That was my first exposure to it."

Broughton has developed an app to help tackle issues with mental health and under-performance in football.

He said the reasons to use nitrous oxide had always been there: pressure on players to perform leaves them searching for an escape.

But Broughton has concerns about the toll nitrous oxide can take.

"I don't think there's the same awareness around nitrous oxide and damage to the body as there would be around alcohol or other drugs," he said.

BBC Sport has been told that some footballers see laughing gas as an alternative to harder substances because it does not stay in the body's system for more than a few hours.

Luci Hanmer, who works with Lancashire drugs and alcohol support charity 'We Are With You', said a substance like nitrous oxide was hard to detect.

She said: "Anything that you're inhaling, the effects that you're going to feel happen very soon.

"So if you are looking for that escapism, the effects are going to be quick.

"Once ingested, it doesn't last very long within your body compared to some of the other substances which can be detected for quite a number of days.

"So if you're getting a drugs test the next day for example, that won't show up."

Sterling given suspended sentence for dangerous driving

Former Manchester City defender Nedum Onuoha said more support was needed, particularly for players like Sterling who break through young.

Sterling made his debut for Liverpool and England at just 17 - before going on to win four Premier League titles at Manchester City and 82 caps for his country, including the Euro 2020 final at Wembley.

"Look at what's happened to Raheem," he said. "Look at how this led to this moment, a moment which I'm sure he's hugely embarrassed about, because I'm sure he can see how dangerous that was to not just his life, but the lives of so many people who are on the road at the same time.

"But I just don't feel like football is in a position where they think it's important to support people who have issues with nitrous oxide."

The BBC Radio 5 live pundit said the use of nitrous oxide in professional footballing circles was very common.

"I think the difference from when I was younger is that people would openly party in certain places," he said.

"Now they party where they're harder to spot. That's why you don't really see on a week-to-week basis now the scandal of somebody that's been out drinking.

"The players are doing it, but it's more sophisticated in terms of how they do it, the locations, and this is an example here with nitrous oxide."

Neurologist Dr Nicholl has been working with patients who have abused nitrous oxide for years and issued a warning to others.

"It certainly is being used by footballers, but it's pretty much the worst thing that you want to be using if you're a professional sportsperson," he said.

"It damages your spinal cord and the spinal cord is a bit like an electrical cable, where the insulation - the outside of that cable - gets stripped away.

"So what patients will complain of is difficulty with feeling on their hands or feet, or unable to walk at all.

"So, in effect, it's like a spinal cord injury. But they can also get blood clots, deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary emboli, and some patients have died."

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line website.

James Dean Bradfield said their rock songs about banking, environmental damage and ideology still have relevance today after three decades

Manic Street Preachers frontman James Dean Bradfield said playing in Wales brings "extra pressure" as the band prepare to mark 35 years of their debut album.

The band will headline Blackweir Fields in Cardiff next summer, performing the landmark 1992 record Generation Terrorists in full.

Bradfield said their rock songs about banking, environmental damage and ideology still "have a prescience for anything you could talk about now".

He said when the band wrote the album, which sold 250,000 copies worldwide upon its release, they were "a bit unreasonable and a bit mad" but also "fiercely ambitious".

Bradfield, raised in Blackwood, Caerphilly, said the album was shaped by the decline of the south Wales valleys after pit closures, channeling their surroundings into songs such as Nat West-Barclays-Midlands-Lloyds, Slash N Burn and Crucifix Kiss.

While discussing Nat West-Barclays-Midlands-Lloyds, he said: "That song has a prescient nature about it and it always will.

"Even though it dates itself, you can take some of the songs and you can actually trace them over the times that we live in now."

Bradfield joked that he and his band mates Nicky Wire, Sean Moore and the late Richey Edwards were "fun to hang out with, I promise you".

Sean Moore, James Dean Bradfield and Nicky Wire have been a three-piece lineup since 1995. Their forth band member Richey Edwards disappeared in February of that year

The album also features Little Baby Nothing, which Bradfield originally envisioned Kylie Minogue singing.

"She did sing on stage with us once in the Shepherd's Bush Empire. I think that was during the Everything Must Go tour, and she was brilliant," he said.

Previously, Bradfield translated one of their songs from their fifth album, This Is My Truth Tell Me Yours, into Welsh for a S4C music series.

"It was a challenge to sing Ready for Drowning in Welsh, definitely," he said.

"I tried to do the lyrics justice in Welsh as much as it had been done justice in English.

"I tried to keep it as poetic as possible rather than just the facts."

Fans told to expect Nicky Wire "to really be rocking the leopard print more than you could imagine"

Bradfield said playing at home in Wales was "a privilege" but came with "more pressure" than gigs elsewhere.

"You can't hide away from the fact that there's more pressure and there's a lot more tension around a hometown gig.

"All those pressures add into making it, it feels like there's more at stake.

"You might see people on the dog walk that came to the concert the night before," he said, laughing.

"You don't want them to give you a bad review when you're getting a coffee with your dog."

He also admitted that he sometimes worries about the prospect of family members being in the crowd and swearing on stage.

"One of my uncles or aunties are going to be in the crowd and I better watch my language. And you're thinking, what am I talking about? I'm in a band," he said.

Asked which songs younger fans should start with, Bradfield picked Crucifix Kiss, Nat West-Barclays-Midlands-Lloyds and So Dead, a song they have never played live.

"Those three songs in themselves, I think, still have a prescience for anything you could talk about now."

L-R Richey Edwards, James Dean Bradfield, Nicky Wire and Sean Moore

Discussing their one-night performance in June 2027, Bradfield said he felt "nervous" about playing the full album and had already started rehearsing.

"I think they can expect a band that's very, very tight, pretty aggressive, but we're going to be on message in terms of the record that we're representing."

He added: "It's going to be very faithful."

Bradfield told fans to expect Wire "to really be rocking the leopard print more than you could imagine."

The Libertines, The Cardigans and The Tub will be supporting the band on Saturday 19 June 2027.

He added: "We've got to try and find a way to honour Richey as well."

Edwards, from Blackwood, disappeared on 1 February 1995.

His car was found abandoned near the old Severn Bridge , but no trace of him has ever been found, and he was declared legally dead in 2008.
